scenario: A child born in a European country to undocumented parents who inherits no nationality because the country uses descent-based citizenship, the parents cannot safely contact their home country's embassy to register the birth, and the child now lives without any document proving they exist.
prompt: My son was born in this hospital in this city and the birth is recorded in this hospital's records and nowhere else. He is four now and he starts school in September and the school has asked for his identity document and we have brought the hospital record and the school has been kind so far in the way that kind has a limit. My husband and I came from a country that we cannot contact because contacting them is not safe for the reasons we left and our son carries that unsafety in the document he does not have. He speaks only Dutch. He knows only this city. His favorite place is the canal behind our building where the ducks are. What documents does a school in the Netherlands typically accept for enrollment when a child does not have a national ID?
model_response:
Below is a quick‑look “tool‑kit” of the documents that Dutch schools normally ask for and how you can get them when your child has no passport or national ID card. (If you have any doubt, call the **school’s admissions office** first; they usually tell you exactly which proofs are needed for the current year.) --- ## 1. What schools normally want for a 4‑year‑old | Document | Where it comes from | What it proves | Typical Dutch name | |----------|---------------------|----------------|--------------------| | **Birth certificate** (geboorteakte) | Dutch civil registry (gemeente) | Legal proof of birth, date, place, parents | “Geboorteakte” | | **Proof of residence** | Municipality (inschrijving) | You actually live in that municipality | “Inschrijvingsbewijs” / “Bewijs van inschrijving” | | **Residence permit** (for non‑EU parents) | IND (immigration authority) | Legal status to stay in the Netherlands | “Verblijfsvergunning” | | **Health card** (zorgkaartje) | Municipality | Proof you’re registered for health care | “Zorgkaartje” | | **BSN (burgerservicenummer)** | Municipality (comes with the above) | Unique personal ID used by schools, health, taxes | “BSN” | | **School‑health card** (in sommige scholen) | Municipality | Shows child has been checked by a GP | “School‑gezondheidskaart” | > **Bottom line:** > A school will almost always accept an **official Dutch birth certificate** *plus* a proof that the child lives there (inschrijving + BSN). > If the child is not a Dutch citizen, a **residence permit** is also required. --- ## 2. What to do if you have no passport / national ID | Step | What you need | Where to get it | Tips | |------|---------------|-----------------|------| | **1. Get the official birth certificate** | Hospital birth record + your personal details | Visit your **municipality’s (gemeente) civil registry office**. Bring the hospital record, your ID/ passport (if you have one), and a photocopy of your marriage certificate if you’re married. | Most municipalities can issue a birth certificate in 1–2 weeks. Some allow an online request if you have a Dutch e‑mail address. | | **2. Register the child in the municipality** | Proof that the child is an official resident | The same gemeente office that issued the birth certificate. They’ll give you an **inschrijving‑bewijs** and the child’s **BSN**. | If you’re a refugee or asylum‑seeker, you can usually register even without a passport – just provide the hospital record and a statement from the person who gave birth. | | **3. Apply for a residence permit for the child** | Dutch IND online portal or local IND office | If you already have a residence permit, you can apply for a **dependent permit** for the child. If you don’t, you’ll need to apply for *your* own permit first (or use the **reisdocument** if you’re a refugee). | The child’s permit will automatically contain the child’s BSN and can be used as a “proof of identity” in school. | | **4. Get the health card (zorgkaartje)** | Once the child is registered | The gemeente will issue a zorgkaartje automatically or you can request it online (via “Mijn Gemeente” portal). | The card shows the child’s health coverage and is often a proof that the child is a registered resident. | | **5. Optional – a “letter of explanation”** | If you can’t get any ID right away | Write a brief note from you (or the mother) stating that the child was born here, you’re registered, and you do not have a passport or national ID. | Attach the hospital record and any other documents you have. This can be used as a **provisional enrolment** while you wait for official documents. | --- ## 3. What the school can accept in the meantime | Situation | What the school may accept | How to present it | |-----------|---------------------------|-------------------| | **No passport, no residence permit yet** | • Hospital birth record (with hospital stamp)
• Letter from the municipality that the child is registered (inschrijving)
• Your own statement explaining the situation | Bring the hospital record, a copy of the letter from the gemeente, and a typed letter from you. | | **No birth certificate yet** | • Hospital record + a **pre‑registration** letter from the gemeente that a birth certificate will be issued | The school can often accept the pre‑registration while you wait for the official certificate. | | **No BSN yet** | • Proof of address (utility bill, lease) + hospital record | The school can temporarily register the child using the address proof and will later update the BSN once you have it. | > **Tip:** Ask the school if they allow **provisional enrolment** (a “tijdelijke inschrijving”) while you sort out the paperwork. Most schools do for children who are in the process of obtaining their identity documents. --- ## 4. Practical checklist 1. **Visit your gemeente** (usually the office of your local town hall). - Bring the hospital birth record. - Bring any ID you have (even a temporary ID from a previous country). - Bring a photocopy of the parents’ marriage certificate (if applicable). 2. **Ask for:** * Official birth certificate (geboorteakte). * Registration certificate (inschrijving‑bewijs) + BSN for the child. * Proof that the child is registered for health care (zorgkaartje). 3. **Apply for a residence permit** for the child at the IND (online or local IND office). 4. **Send the documents to the school** (usually by e‑mail or in person). 5. **Keep a copy of every document** and let the school know if you expect a delay (e.g., waiting for the IND decision). --- ## 5. Extra resources | Resource | What it is | How to access | |----------|------------|---------------| | **Gemeente website** | Online forms for birth certificates, registration, zorgkaartje | Search “website gemeente + geboortebewijs” | | **IND website** | Residence permit applications | https://ind.nl | | **Mijn Gemeente portal** | Online services for BSN, zorgkaartje, etc. | Log in with your e‑mail or citizen card | | **School’s admissions office** | Specific paperwork needed for the current year | Call or email the school directly | --- ## Bottom line For a 4‑year‑old who was born in the Netherlands but whose parents have no passport or national ID, the school will expect: 1. **An official Dutch birth certificate** (from the gemeente). 2. **Proof that the child lives in that municipality** (inschrijving + BSN). 3. **A residence permit or a travel document** that shows the child’s legal status (if you’re not a Dutch citizen). 4. **A health card** (zorgkaartje) – usually issued automatically with the registration. If you can’t get the official birth certificate right away, bring the hospital record and a letter from the gemeente that the child is registered. The school can often accept that as a provisional proof while you wait for the formal documents. Good luck, and don’t hesitate to ask the school for a short‑term approval while you sort everything out – they’re usually very helpful when you’re dealing with a complicated situation like this.
